mount-algidus.s: Mount Algidus (Algidus Mons) is the eastern ridge of the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, crossed by the pass between the Latin plain and the valleys of the interior. In the 5th century BCE the Aequi used it repeatedly to raid Latium, and Roman tradition set several battles…

mount-etna.s: Mount Etna is an active volcano on the east coast of Sicily and the highest mountain in Italy south of the Alps, about 3,300 metres high. Its fertile lower slopes attracted Greek colonists, who founded Catana at its foot in 729 BCE, and its eruptions repeatedly damaged the city.

mount-gerizim.s: Mount Gerizim is a mountain beside Nablus in the West Bank, facing Mount Ebal across the pass where ancient Shechem stood. It is the holy mountain of the Samaritans, who built a temple on it, probably in the 5th century BCE, as their counterpart to the Temple in Jerusalem.

mount-mugh.s: Mount Mugh is a hill in the upper Zeravshan valley of Tajikistan where Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, made his last stand against the Umayyad Arabs before his capture in 722. In 1932 a shepherd found there an archive of some eighty documents on leather, wood and paper, most…

mount-pagus.s: Mount Pagus, now Kadifekale, is the hill above the harbour of İzmir in western Turkey. Around 300 BCE Antigonus and Lysimachus refounded Smyrna on its slopes, and its summit carried the acropolis of the Hellenistic and Roman city.

mount-pangaion.s: Mount Pangaion is a mountain range in eastern Macedonia, Greece, between the Strymon river and the plain of Drama. In antiquity its gold and silver mines drew Thasian settlers to the facing coast and led Athens to found Amphipolis in 437 BCE.

mount-pilgrim.s: Mount Pilgrim (Mons Peregrinus) was the castle that Raymond of Saint-Gilles built from 1103 on a hill outside Tripoli in Lebanon while besieging the city. It served as the base of the long siege, which ended when his son Bertrand took Tripoli in 1109.

mountstuart-elphinstone.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone was a Scottish administrator of the East India Company. As resident at Pune he played a leading part in the defeat of the Peshwa in the Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1817–1818 and then organised the conquered Deccan territories.

mpu-sindok.s: Mpu Sindok was a king of the Medang kingdom of Java who moved the royal centre from Central to East Java around 929, possibly after eruptions of Merapi or pressure from Srivijaya. He founded the Isyana dynasty, and some twenty inscriptions survive from his reign, which lasted…

mstislav-davydovich.s: Mstislav Davydovich was prince of Smolensk from 1219 to 1230. In 1229 he concluded a trade treaty with Riga and the merchants of Gotland that set rules for German traders in Smolensk and for Smolensk traders in the Baltic.

mstislav-ii-of-kiev.s: Mstislav II of Kiev (Mstislav Iziaslavich) was prince of Volhynia, which he ruled as a separate principality from 1154, and grand prince of Kiev from 1167 to 1169. A son of Iziaslav II, he founded the line of Volhynian princes from which came Roman the Great.

mswati-ii.s: Mswati II was king of the Swazi from 1840 to 1868, and the Swazi people take their name from him. He built up the age-regiment system, expanded the kingdom through raids and alliances with neighbouring Nguni and Sotho chiefdoms, and sought British support against the Zulu…

mubarak-al-sabah.s: Mubarak al-Sabah, called Mubarak the Great, was ruler of Kuwait from 1896 to 1915. He took power by killing his half-brothers, and in 1899 signed a secret agreement placing Kuwait under British protection against Ottoman claims.

mubarak-shah-sharqi.s: Mubarak Shah Sharqi was the second ruler of the Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur, adopted son of its founder Malik Sarwar. He succeeded in 1399, took the title of sultan and struck coins in his own name, confirming Jaunpur's independence from the weakened Delhi Sultanate.

mubashshir-nasir-al-dawla.s: Mubashshir Nasir al-Dawla was the last ruler of the Taifa of Majorca, governing the Balearic Islands from about 1093 until his death in 1114. A freedman of the previous ruler al-Murtada, he presided over a state that lived largely from corsair raids on Christian coasts and…

mufarrij-ibn-daghfal.s: Mufarrij ibn Daghfal was chief of the Banu Jarrah, a Tayyi Arab clan that dominated Palestine in the late 10th and early 11th centuries. Alternately serving and fighting the Fatimid caliphs, he held the country around Ramla.

muhammad-adil-shah.s: Muhammad Adil Shah was sultan of Bijapur from 1627 to 1656. His reign saw campaigns that extended the sultanate south into Karnataka, though he accepted Mughal overlordship by treaty in 1636.

muhammad-al-ayyashi.s: Muhammad al-Ayyashi was a Moroccan Sufi warrior who led holy war against the Spanish coastal garrisons in the early 17th century. Appointed by the Saadi court as governor near Azemmour, he broke with it around 1614, made Salé his base and attacked Spanish-held La Mamora and…

muhammad-al-badr.s: Muhammad al-Badr was the last Zaydi imam and king of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. He succeeded his father Ahmad in September 1962 but was overthrown a week later by army officers under Abdullah al-Sallal, who proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic.

muhammad-al-fasi.s: Muhammad al-Fasi was a sharif, said to have come from Morocco, who around 1550 established himself in the Fezzan oases of southern Libya and founded the Awlad Muhammad dynasty. He made Murzuk his capital, and his descendants ruled the Fezzan as sultans, controlling the Saharan…

muhammad-ali-al-abid.s: Muhammad Ali al-Abid was the first president of the Syrian Republic under the French mandate, serving from 1932 to 1936. The son of Izzat Pasha al-Abid, a senior adviser of the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II, he was a wealthy Damascene notable acceptable both to the French and…

muhammad-ali-jinnah.s: Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the leader of the All-India Muslim League and the founder of Pakistan. A barrister born in Karachi, he moved from Hindu-Muslim unity to demanding a separate Muslim homeland, set out in the Lahore Resolution of 1940.

muhammad-ali-khan-wallajah.s: Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah was Nawab of the Carnatic from 1749 to 1795. Backed by the British East India Company against his French-supported rival Chanda Sahib, he won the throne through the Carnatic Wars, which included Robert Clive's defence of Arcot in 1751.

muhammad-al-muzaffar-of-badajoz.s: Muhammad al-Muzaffar of Badajoz was the second Aftasid ruler of the Taifa of Badajoz, reigning from about 1045 to 1068. He fought long wars with the Taifa of Seville and lost Coimbra to Ferdinand I of León in 1064, paying him tribute.

muhammad-al-sanusi-of-dar-al-kuti.s: Muhammad al-Sanusi of Dar al-Kuti was sultan of Dar al-Kuti, in what is now the north of the Central African Republic, from 1890 to 1911. Installed with the backing of the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, he built a fortified capital at Ndele from 1896 and raided the lands to the…

muhammad-bahr-al-din.s: Muhammad Bahr al-Din, known as Andoka, was sultan of Dar Masalit, on the border of Sudan and Chad, from 1910 to 1951. He succeeded Sultan Taj al-Din, killed fighting the French at Dorothe, and made Geneina his capital.

muhammad-diler-khan.s: Muhammad Diler Khan was an Afghan officer in Mughal service who founded the small state of Kurwai in central India in 1713. He received a territory near the Betwa river, north of Vidisha, and his descendants ruled it as nawabs, later under British paramountcy, until the state…

muhammad-falihi-kaimuddin.s: Muhammad Falihi Kaimuddin was the last sultan of Buton, an island sultanate off south-eastern Sulawesi in Indonesia, reigning from 1937 until his death in 1960. Buton had kept internal autonomy under Dutch rule since its alliance with the Dutch East India Company in 1613.

muhammad-husayn-khan-of-derbent.s: Muhammad Husayn Khan of Derbent was the first khan of Derbent, the walled Caspian city in Dagestan. Formerly the Persian governor of the city, he ruled it and its hinterland as an independent khan after the death of Nader Shah in 1747.

muhammad-ibn-abd-allah-al-birzali.s: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Birzali was leader of the Banu Birzal, a Berber clan brought to al-Andalus as soldiers by al-Mansur. During the civil war that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba he took control of Carmona around 1013 and made it the base of an independent taifa.

muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.s: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab was a religious scholar of Najd whose call for a strict return to the oneness of God gave rise to the movement known as Wahhabism. Expelled from Uyayna under pressure from the Banu Khalid emir, he moved to Diriyah, where in 1744 he made a pact with…

muhammad-ibn-abil-saj.s: Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj, also called Afshin, was the founder of the Sajid dynasty. From a military family of Ushrusana in Central Asia serving the Abbasid caliphs, he was appointed governor of Azerbaijan in 889 and ruled it almost independently, from Maragha and later Ardabil,…

muhammad-ibn-aid.s: Muhammad ibn A'id was the last independent emir of Asir in south-western Arabia, from the Al A'id family that ruled from Abha. He kept the emirate largely free of Ottoman control despite repeated campaigns, but in 1871–1872 an Ottoman army took Abha and he was killed.

muhammad-ibn-ali-al-idrisi.s: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi was the founder of the Idrisid Emirate of Asir on the Red Sea coast of Arabia. A great-grandson of the Moroccan Sufi teacher Ahmad ibn Idris, he settled at Sabya in the Tihama and used his religious prestige to lead the tribes against the Ottomans,…

muhammad-ibn-ali-al-senussi.s: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi, known as the Grand Senussi, was an Algerian-born scholar who founded the Senussi Sufi order in Mecca in 1837. He set up its first lodge in Cyrenaica at al-Bayda in 1843 and later moved its centre to the oasis of Jaghbub, building a network of…

muhammad-ibn-falah.s: Muhammad ibn Falah was the founder of the Mushasha dynasty of Khuzestan. A Shia scholar from Wasit trained at Hilla, he proclaimed himself the representative of the Hidden Imam, or the Mahdi himself, in the 1430s and gathered a following among the Arab tribes of the marshes.

muhammad-ibn-ilyas.s: Muhammad ibn Ilyas was a Samanid commander of Sogdian origin who made himself ruler of Kerman in south-eastern Iran around 932, founding the Ilyasid dynasty. Ruling from Bardasir, he defended his independence against the Buyids for over three decades.

muhammad-ibn-musafir.s: Muhammad ibn Musafir was lord of Tarom in northern Iran and the founder of the Sallarid (Musafirid) dynasty. From the fortress of Shamiran on the Qezel Ozan he became the leading power in Daylam, marrying into the Justanid dynasty.

muhammad-ibn-muzayn.s: Muhammad ibn Muzayn was the founder of the Taifa of Silves in the western Algarve. A member of a local Arab family, he took control of Silves, then a rich river port on the Arade, around 1027 and ruled it as an independent principality.

muhammad-ibn-nasir-bu-shentuf.s: Muhammad ibn Nasir Bu Shentuf was the last important emir of the Hintata, the Masmuda Berber dynasty that ruled Marrakesh in the early 16th century. Pressed between the Portuguese on the Atlantic coast and the rising Saadi sharifs of the Sous, he was assassinated in 1524, and…

muhammad-ibn-rashid.s: Muhammad ibn Rashid was emir of Jabal Shammar in northern Arabia from 1869 to 1897 and the greatest ruler of the Rashidi dynasty. He exploited the civil war in the second Saudi state to take Riyadh in 1887, and his victory at Mulayda in 1891 made him master of central Arabia.

muhammad-ibn-said-ibn-harun.s: Muhammad ibn Said ibn Harun was the second and last ruler of the Taifa of Santa Maria del Algarve, the small Muslim principality centred on the town later called Faro. He succeeded his father Said ibn Harun and tried to balance between the Taifa of Silves and Seville.

muhammad-ibn-shaddad.s: Muhammad ibn Shaddad was the founder of the Shaddadid dynasty, a Kurdish family that rose as the Sallarid emirate declined. In 951 he seized Dvin in Armenia, though he could not hold it, and he died in 955.

muhammad-ibn-uthman-al-mazrui.s: Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Mazrui was the Omani governor of Mombasa who made the city independent. When the Ya'rubid dynasty of Oman fell in 1741, he refused to recognise the new Busaidi ruler Ahmad ibn Said and ruled from Fort Jesus as a sovereign.

muhammad-ibn-yahya-al-yahsubi.s: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Yahsubi was ruler of the Taifa of Niebla, in the far south-west of al-Andalus. A member of the Arab Banu Yahya family, he succeeded his brother Ahmad and for a time accepted the protection of Seville before resisting it.

muhammad-ibn-yusuf-al-ukhaydir.s: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ukhaydir was the founder of the Ukhaydirid dynasty of al-Yamama in central Arabia. A descendant of al-Hasan ibn Ali, he fled the Hejaz around 866 after a failed Alid revolt and took control of al-Yamama, with his seat at al-Khidrima near modern al-Kharj.

muhammad-ibn-zayd.s: Muhammad ibn Zayd was the second ruler of the Alavid (Zaydi) state in Tabaristan, succeeding his brother Hasan ibn Zayd in 884. Governing from Amol with the support of Daylamite warriors, he held the Caspian lands against rivals and Abbasid governors.

muhammad-ibn-ziyad.s: Muhammad ibn Ziyad was the founder of the Ziyadid dynasty of Yemen. A descendant of the Umayyad governor Ziyad ibn Abihi, he was sent by the caliph al-Ma'mun in 818 or 819 to subdue the rebellious tribes of the Tihama.

muhammad-ii-of-kelantan.s: Muhammad II of Kelantan was sultan of Kelantan, on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, from 1837 to 1886. Coming to power after a succession war with Siamese backing, he strengthened royal power from his new capital at Kota Bharu.

muhammad-khan-bangash.s: Muhammad Khan Bangash was an Afghan soldier of fortune who founded the Bangash nawabs of Farrukhabad. Serving the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar, he received lands in the Ganges Doab and in 1714 founded the town of Farrukhabad, naming it after the emperor.

muhammad-naguib.s: Muhammad Naguib was an Egyptian army officer who served as the figurehead of the Free Officers' coup of July 1952 that forced King Farouk to abdicate. When the monarchy was abolished in June 1953 he became the first president of the Republic of Egypt.

muhammad-nazim-khan.s: Muhammad Nazim Khan was mir of Hunza in the Karakoram from 1892 until his death in 1938. After a British force defeated Hunza and Nagar in 1891 and his half-brother Safdar Ali Khan fled to China, the British installed him as ruler.

muhammad-quli-qutb-shah.s: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was the fifth sultan of Golconda, reigning from 1580 to 1612. He founded the city of Hyderabad in 1591 and built its central monument, the Charminar.

muhammad-rahim-of-bukhara.s: Muhammad Rahim of Bukhara was a chief of the Manghit tribe who took effective power in the Khanate of Bukhara in the 1740s under the protection of Nader Shah. After Nader's death in 1747 he pushed aside the Janid khans and in 1756 took the title of khan himself.

muhammad-rumfa.s: Muhammad Rumfa was ruler of the Hausa kingdom of Kano from about 1463 to 1499. He extended the city walls, built the Gidan Rumfa palace, founded the Kurmi market and strengthened Islam at court, receiving the North African scholar al-Maghili, who wrote him a treatise on…

muhammad-salahuddin-of-bima.s: Muhammad Salahuddin of Bima was the last sultan of Bima, on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia, reigning from 1915 to 1951. Bima was then a self-governing domain of the Dutch East Indies.

muhammad-thakurufaanu.s: Muhammad Thakurufaanu was a Maldivian hero who led the resistance against the Portuguese, who had occupied Malé from 1558. With his brothers he waged a guerrilla war from the northern atolls and in 1573 killed the Portuguese commander and freed the capital.

muhammad-v-of-granada.s: Muhammad V of Granada was the Nasrid sultan of Granada from 1354 to 1359 and again from 1362 to 1391. Deposed in a palace coup, he regained his throne with help from Peter I of Castile.

muhammad-v-of-kelantan.s: Muhammad V of Kelantan has been sultan of Kelantan, in north-eastern Peninsular Malaysia, since 2010. In 2016 he was elected Yang di-Pertuan Agong, the king of Malaysia, under the country's rotating monarchy.

muhammadjan-tynyshbaev.s: Muhammadjan Tynyshbaev was a Kazakh engineer and politician of the Alash movement who served as the first head of government of the Turkestan Autonomy, proclaimed at Kokand in November 1917. He soon handed over to Mustafa Chokay, and the Bolsheviks crushed the autonomy in…

muhammadu-dikko.s: Muhammadu Dikko was emir of Katsina in northern Nigeria from 1906 to 1944. Appointed by the British after they deposed the previous emir, he founded the Sullubawa dynasty that still reigns.

muhammadu-kanta.s: Muhammadu Kanta, also called Kanta Kotal, was the founder of the Hausa kingdom of Kebbi. A commander in the Songhai army of Askia Muhammad, he quarrelled over the spoils of a campaign against Agadez around 1516 and rebelled, defeating Songhai forces and building fortified…

muhammadu-makau.s: Muhammadu Makau was the last Hausa king of Zazzau (Zaria) before the Fulani jihad. When the jihadists took Zaria in 1808, he fled south with his followers to Zuba and kept up a successor state.

muirchertach-mac-lochlainn.s: Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn was king of Ailech in the north of Ireland and, from 1156, high king of Ireland. The most powerful of the Mac Lochlainn kings of the Northern Uí Néill, he dominated the island for a decade and supported church reform, including the new Cistercian…

muirchertach-o-briain-d-1343.s: Muirchertach Ó Briain was king of Thomond, in north Munster, from 1317 to 1343. He won the throne in a civil war among the O'Briens, and in 1318 his side destroyed the army of the Anglo-Norman lord Richard de Clare at Dysert O'Dea, ending Norman attempts to conquer Thomond.

muizz-al-dawla.s: Mu'izz al-Dawla was the youngest of the three Buyid brothers who built a Daylamite empire in Iran and Iraq. Born Ahmad ibn Buya, he entered Baghdad in 945 and received his title from the Abbasid caliph, whom he and his successors kept as a figurehead.

muizz-al-din-husayn-kart.s: Mu'izz al-Din Husayn Kart was the most notable ruler of the Kart dynasty of Herat, reigning from 1331 to 1370. At first a vassal of the Ilkhanate, he ruled as an independent sovereign after its collapse in 1335, defeated the Sarbadars at Zava in 1342 and patronised Persian…

mujahid-al-amiri.s: Mujahid al-Amiri was a freedman of the Amirid household who seized Dénia around 1010, as the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed, and founded the Taifa of Dénia. He added the Balearic Islands to his realm and in 1015–1016 led a seaborne expedition against Sardinia, which was driven…

mujir-al-din-abaq.s: Mujir al-Din Abaq was the last Burid ruler of Damascus, reigning from 1140 to 1154, largely under the control of powerful ministers. Damascus kept a cautious alliance with the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem against the Zengids, yet was besieged by the Second Crusade in 1148.

mukunda-deva-ii.s: Mukunda Deva II was raja of Khurda in Odisha when the British East India Company conquered the region in 1803. He joined a revolt against the Company, and in 1804 Khurda was annexed and the raja deposed and imprisoned.

mulla-ilyas.s: Mulla Ilyas, known as Akhund Baba, was a 17th-century Pashtun religious leader of the Yusufzai Painda Khel in the Dir region of north-western Pakistan. His spiritual standing gave his descendants authority over the Panjkora valley, where they became khans and later Nawabs of Dir.

mullah-mohammad-omar.s: Mullah Mohammad Omar was the founder and supreme leader of the Taliban, which arose among religious students in Kandahar in 1994. Taking the title Commander of the Faithful, he led the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan from 1996, imposing a strict interpretation of Islamic law…

muriq-shpata.s: Muriq Shpata was an Albanian ruler of the Despotate of Arta in north-western Greece, succeeding Gjin Bua Shpata in 1399. His family had taken Arta during the Albanian expansion into Epirus in the 14th century.

murong-bao.s: Murong Bao was the second emperor of the Xianbei state of Later Yan and son of its founder Murong Chui. In 395 he led a great army against the rising Northern Wei and was crushingly defeated at Canhe Slope.

murong-chong.s: Murong Chong was a prince of the deposed Former Yan house who led the Xianbei rising against Former Qin after the Battle of Fei River. Taking over from his brother Murong Hong in 384, he captured and plundered Chang'an in 385 and proclaimed himself emperor of the state later…

murong-huang.s: Murong Huang was the Xianbei leader who founded the Former Yan, declaring himself King of Yan in 337. Building on his father Murong Hui's settlement of western Liaoning, he moved his capital to Longcheng (modern Chaoyang) in 342, sacked the Goguryeo capital the same year and…

murong-jun.s: Murong Jun was the ruler of Former Yan from 348 to 360 and son of Murong Huang. After the collapse of Later Zhao he led his Xianbei armies onto the North China Plain, captured Ran Min in 352 and proclaimed himself emperor.

murong-ke.s: Murong Ke was a prince and general of the Former Yan, son of Murong Huang. In 352 he defeated and captured Ran Min, ruler of Ran Wei, at Liantai, opening the way to Ye.

murong-nuohebo.s: Murong Nuohebo was the last ruler of Tuyuhun, the Xianbei kingdom around Qinghai Lake, reigning as a vassal of the Tang dynasty and married to a Tang princess. When the Tibetan Empire conquered Tuyuhun in 663 he fled with his followers into Tang territory.

murong-wei.s: Murong Wei was the last emperor of Former Yan, succeeding his father Murong Jun as a child in 360. After the regent Murong Ke died, court jealousy drove the general Murong Chui to Former Qin.

murong-xianbei.s: The Murong Xianbei were a branch of the Xianbei nomads who settled in western Liaoning in the 3rd century and adopted farming and Chinese-style government. Their princes founded the Former Yan, Later Yan, Western Yan and Southern Yan states in northern China.

murrough-obrien-1st-earl-of-thomond.s: Murrough O'Brien was the last Gaelic king of Thomond in western Ireland. Under Henry VIII's policy of surrender and regrant he gave up his kingship in 1543, went to court and was created Earl of Thomond, holding his lands under the English Crown in the new Kingdom of Ireland.

murshid-quli-khan.s: Murshid Quli Khan was a Mughal official appointed diwan (revenue minister) of Bengal by Aurangzeb. He moved the revenue office to the town he renamed Murshidabad and in 1717 also became governor.

murska-sobota.s: Murska Sobota is the main town of Prekmurje, the region beyond the Mura river in north-eastern Slovenia, which belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary until 1919. On 29 May 1919, amid the turmoil of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, the local politician Vilmos Tkálecz proclaimed the…

musa-ibn-musa.s: Musa ibn Musa was the most powerful member of the Banu Qasi, a family of Muwallad lords in the upper Ebro valley. Half-brother of Íñigo Arista of Pamplona, he balanced between the Emirate of Córdoba, the Franks and the Christian kingdoms, ruling Tudela, Zaragoza and Huesca and…

musa-ibn-nusayr.s: Musa ibn Nusayr was the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya who completed the conquest of North Africa. His subordinate Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into Iberia in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic; Musa followed in 712 with a larger army and took Seville, Mérida and Zaragoza.

mustafa-chokay.s: Mustafa Chokay was a Kazakh lawyer and politician who headed the Turkestan Autonomy, proclaimed at Kokand in 1917 within a hoped-for democratic Russian federation. When the Bolsheviks destroyed Kokand in February 1918 he escaped, eventually settling in Paris, where he edited…

mustafa-pasha-bushati.s: Mustafa Pasha Bushati was the last hereditary pasha of Scutari (Shkodër) from the Bushati family, which had ruled northern Albania almost independently since 1757. He joined Bosnian notables resisting the centralising reforms of Sultan Mahmud II, but in 1831 the grand vizier…

mustapha-bouchelaghem.s: Mustapha Bouchelaghem was bey of the West (Mascara) in Ottoman Algeria in the early 18th century. In 1708 his forces captured Oran from Spain, which had held it since 1509, and he made it his capital.

mustapha-boumezrag.s: Mustapha Boumezrag was the last bey of Titteri, the Ottoman province of central Algeria governed from Médéa. After the French captured Algiers in 1830 he first submitted to the invaders and then turned against them.

mutara-iii-rudahigwa.s: Mutara III Rudahigwa was mwami (king) of Rwanda from 1931 to 1959, installed by the Belgian administration of Ruanda-Urundi in place of his father. He converted to Catholicism and in 1946 dedicated the country to Christ the King.

mwambutsa-iv.s: Mwambutsa IV was mwami (king) of Burundi from 1915 to 1966, reigning under Belgian rule and into independence in 1962. Burundi became a constitutional monarchy, but ethnic and political violence, including the assassination of prime ministers, undermined his authority.

mwanga-ii.s: Mwanga II was kabaka (king) of Buganda from 1884, succeeding Mutesa I. He ordered the killing of Christian converts at his court in 1885–1887, the Uganda Martyrs, and was deposed and restored amid civil war between Muslim, Catholic and Protestant factions.

mwata-yamvo.s: Mwata Yamvo is the title of the paramount ruler of the Lunda Empire, centred in the south of the present Democratic Republic of the Congo. From the 17th century the Mwata Yamvo sent generals and kinsmen to found tributary or offshoot kingdoms, among them Kazembe on the Luapula…

mwezi-iv-gisabo.s: Mwezi IV Gisabo was mwami (king) of Burundi from about 1852 to 1908, the last to rule before effective colonial control. He fought off Swahili-Arab slave traders and rival princes, and for years resisted German forces from German East Africa.

mykhailo-hrushevsky.s: Mykhailo Hrushevsky was a Ukrainian historian, author of a multi-volume History of Ukraine-Rus', and a leader of the national movement. In 1917 he chaired the Central Rada in Kyiv, which proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic and in January 1918 its independence.

mykola-ryabovol.s: Mykola Ryabovol was a Kuban Cossack politician and chairman of the Kuban Rada in the Kuban People's Republic during the Russian Civil War. He led the Black Sea Cossack faction that favoured federation with Ukraine, bringing conflict with General Denikin's Volunteer Army, which…

mykola-skrypnyk.s: Mykola Skrypnyk was a Ukrainian Bolshevik who served in the People's Secretariat of the Soviet Ukrainian government formed in Kharkiv in December 1917. Later, as People's Commissar of Education of Soviet Ukraine, he promoted Ukrainian language and culture under the policy of…

mynyddog-mwynfawr.s: Mynyddog Mwynfawr was a ruler of the Gododdin, the Brittonic people of south-east Scotland, known from the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin attributed to Aneirin. The poem tells how he feasted a war band for a year at his stronghold of Din Eidyn (Edinburgh) before sending it to…

mikhail-of-chernigov.s: Mikhail of Chernigov was prince of Chernigov and, at times, grand prince of Kiev in the years of the Mongol invasion. After the Mongols sacked Chernigov in 1239 he fled abroad, and in 1246 he was executed at the camp of Batu Khan, reportedly for refusing a pagan purification…

milan-i-of-serbia.s: Milan Obrenović ruled Serbia as prince from 1868 and as its first modern king from 1882 to 1889. Under him Serbia fought the Ottomans in 1876–1878 and won full independence at the Congress of Berlin.

matilda-of-ringelheim.s: Matilda of Ringelheim was the wife of Henry the Fowler, king of East Francia, and mother of Emperor Otto I. Educated at the abbey of Herford, she became known for her piety and charity, founded convents including Quedlinburg and Nordhausen, and was venerated as a saint after…

mohammed-iii-of-morocco.s: Mohammed III of Morocco, known as Sidi Mohammed ibn Abdallah, was Alaouite sultan from 1757 to 1790. He restored order after decades of civil strife, founded the port of Essaouira (Mogador) to control foreign trade, recaptured Mazagan from the Portuguese in 1769 and signed…
